pool.label: C1
pool.builds_on: The paper demonstrated that a dual heterogenous lamellar microstructure can achieve high strength–ductility synergy by promoting back-stress strengthening at interfaces. This hypothesis extends the concept by chemically strengthening these boundaries using boron segregation.
pool.what_is_new: Instead of relying solely on mechanical processing to induce heterogeneity, this approach uses deliberate chemical intervention (boron doping) to stabilize interfaces and suppress brittle failure, providing an alternative route to improve the strength–ductility balance.

fields.hypothesis: Adding a small amount of boron to the eutectic HEA composition (e.g. AlCoCrFeNi2.1 + ~0.2–0.5 at% B) will promote grain-boundary segregation that both strengthens the interlamellar and intergranular regions and reduces brittle fracture, thereby simultaneously increasing yield strength and ductility.
fields.material_initial_state: As-cast or conventionally processed AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with its inherent lamellar (L12 + B2) microstructure.
fields.intervention: Minor alloying by adding boron during melting to achieve a uniform distribution of boron that segregates to grain and phase boundaries.
fields.conditions: Standard melting and suction-casting methods followed by thermomechanical processing (e.g. hybrid rolling or conventional rolling) at temperatures similar to those in the paper; subsequent tensile testing at room temperature.
fields.structural_mediator: Grain and lamellar boundary chemistry which, when enriched in boron, yields more cohesive interfaces and may also induce a nano-precipitate effect that locally refines the structure.
fields.mechanism: Boron is known in Ni3Al-based alloys to segregate to grain boundaries and suppress intergranular fracture by reducing boundary energy and promoting ductile failure (TXT::wikipedia::Nickel_aluminide::001). In the eutectic HEA, boron is expected to enhance the cohesion of the interfaces between the soft L12 and the hard B2 phases. This should reduce early crack initiation and allow a beneficial accumulation of geometrically necessary dislocations at the heterogeneous interfaces (back-stress strengthening), increasing both strength and ductility.
fields.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline alloy without boron, the boron-doped alloy should show an increase in yield strength and ultimate tensile strength by a moderate fraction (uncertain in magnitude but potentially on the order of 10–20% improvement) as well as an increase in uniform elongation due to improved damage tolerance.
fields.baseline: The eutectic HEA as processed without boron addition (e.g. as-cast or processed with hybrid rolling as in PMC6687781).
fields.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected if boron is added in minor amounts; too high a boron content may lead to the formation of brittle boride phases which could act as crack sources.
fields.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement depends on the solubility limit and segregation behavior of boron in the complex multi-component system; optimal boron level is not precisely known.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of the eutectic HEA with the standard composition and another with an added 0.2–0.5 at% boron. Process both via identical thermo‐mechanical procedures (e.g. hybrid rolling) to achieve similar heterogenous lamellar structures. Conduct tensile tests and microstructural analysis (e.g. TEM/EDS to check boron segregation at boundaries).
measurements: Yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, uniform elongation
Fractography to assess intergranular versus transgranular fracture
Microstructural characterization to check for boride precipitates or changes in boundary chemistry
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-doped samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in both strength and ductility compared to the baseline, or if brittle boride phases form leading to lower ductility, the hypothesis would be falsified.

pool.label: C2
pool.builds_on: the importance of the lamellar architecture and back-stress mechanisms described in the paper.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes controlling the orientation of the lamellae via directional solidification—a processing route not covered in the paper—to further enhance the synergetic strength–ductility effect.

fields.hypothesis: Applying directional solidification to produce a highly aligned, unidirectional lamellar architecture in the eutectic high-entropy alloy will increase both its yield strength and ductility by enhancing back‐stress development and promoting uniform plastic deformation.
fields.material_initial_state: As-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a naturally inherited but somewhat random lamellar orientation.
fields.intervention: Replace the conventional suction-casting process with directional solidification, using a seeded growth technique to orient the lamellae parallel to the loading direction.
fields.conditions: Conduct directional solidification under a controlled high thermal gradient; follow with similar cold-rolling and annealing as in the baseline to preserve the lamellar structure; test tensile properties at room temperature.
fields.structural_mediator: A highly aligned lamellar microstructure that promotes continuous, load-bearing interfaces.
fields.mechanism: A unidirectional lamellar alignment enhances the constraint effect during deformation, leading to a more uniformly distributed back-stress. This reduced heterogeneous deformation minimizes stress concentrations and microcrack formation, thereby increasing both strength and ductility.
fields.predicted_outcome: Compared to conventionally cast alloys, an expected increase in yield strength by a modest percentage (tentative improvement on the order of 10–20%) and similar or improved total ductility due to more homogeneous strain distribution.
fields.baseline: EHEAs produced by suction-casting, as described in the paper (e.g., DPHL700 sample).
fields.boundary: The effect is expected to hold as long as the directional solidification yields a near-identical phase fraction and lamellar spacing; deviations in cooling rate that drastically alter phase distribution may nullify the effect.
fields.uncertainty: Exact quantitative improvements are uncertain and likely depend on the quality of lamella alignment and process parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two sets of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloys: one using conventional suction-casting and the other using directional solidification (with seed orientation control). Process both identically post-solidification (including cold-rolling and annealing).
measurements: Quantitative microstructural characterization (lamella orientation distribution, spacing, phase fractions) using SEM/TEM.
Tensile tests to measure yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation.
In-situ imaging during deformation to observe strain localization.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the directional solidification samples do not show statistically significant higher yield strength and ductility over the control samples, or if the aligned lamellae do not persist post-processing, then the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C3
pool.builds_on: the observation in the paper that the dual-phase lamellar morphology and preserved phase boundaries play a key role in achieving a good strength–ductility balance.
pool.what_is_new: It proposes a processing route (increasing cooling rate to refine lamellae) as a single intervention to further enhance both properties by altering the microstructural scale, rather than modifying the alloy chemistry or secondary treatments.

fields.hypothesis: A controlled increase in the cooling rate during solidification that refines the lamellar spacing can simultaneously improve the strength and ductility of eutectic HEAs by enhancing interface density.
fields.material_initial_state: As-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with lamellar B2 and L12 phases and B2 lamella thickness around ~2 µm.
fields.intervention: Increase the cooling rate during casting to achieve a finer lamellar spacing (smaller interphase distances).
fields.conditions: Processing under conditions amenable to rapid solidification; keeping the overall alloy composition unchanged; experiments at room temperature using standard tensile and compressive tests.
fields.structural_mediator: Increased density of phase boundaries and reduced lamella thickness.
fields.mechanism: Finer lamellar spacing introduces a higher volume fraction of phase boundaries, which serve as barriers to dislocation motion (enhancing strength) and also promote a more uniform distribution of strain by facilitating back-stress effects from closely spaced soft (L12) and hard (B2) phases (improving ductility). This dual role is expected because the refined microstructure enhances strain hardening via increased geometrically necessary dislocations at the interfaces (as seen in the paper’s findings on interface-deformation interactions, PMC7021732::web::019::micro_pillar_compression).
fields.predicted_outcome: Increase in yield strength and work hardening with a moderate improvement or retention of ductility relative to the baseline cast alloy; the magnitude is expected to be on the order of a 15–25% improvement, although precise values are uncertain.
fields.baseline: Standard as-cast microstructure with coarser lamellar spacing (~2 µm B2 lamellae) and the reported strength and ductility values (e.g., tensile UTS ~1165 MPa, ~18% ductility).
fields.boundary: The beneficial effects should persist provided the cooling rate does not induce unwanted microsegregation or phase instabilities; extreme rapid cooling might lead to amorphization or other defects.
fields.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement is uncertain and may vary with specific alloy system sensitivities and cooling conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 samples: one produced with the standard cooling rate (baseline) and one with a significantly increased cooling rate. Characterize the lamellar spacing using SEM/TEM, then perform identical tensile and compressive tests at room temperature.
measurements: Lamellar spacing distribution, phase boundary area per unit volume
Yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and ductility (elongation) in tensile tests
Work hardening rate from stress–strain curves
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the refined lamellar structure sample does not show statistically significant improvements in both strength and ductility over the baseline, or if ductility is compromised despite higher strength, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C4
pool.builds_on: the paper’s insights on phase-specific deformation, particularly the role of the more ductile L12 phase in accommodating plasticity (PMC7021732::web::019::micro_pillar_compression), combined with principles of precipitation strengthening.
pool.what_is_new: It proposes a novel compositional modification (small Ti addition) to deliberately generate beneficial nanoprecipitates within the ductile phase, providing an alternative route to enhance both strength and ductility that was not explored in the paper.

fields.hypothesis: A minor titanium addition to the eutectic HEA can precipitate fine, coherent Ti-rich second-phase particles in the L12 matrix, acting as obstacles to dislocation motion and thus concurrently enhancing strength and ductility.
fields.material_initial_state: As-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy with a microstructure of alternating B2 and L12 phases, where the L12 phase is relatively ductile but contributes less to the overall yield strength.
fields.intervention: Introduce a small amount (e.g., 0.5–1 wt%) of titanium into the alloy during melting.
fields.conditions: Standard melting, casting, and homogenization protocols under an inert atmosphere; subsequent aging (if needed) to promote Ti-rich precipitate formation in the L12 phase; mechanical testing at room temperature.
fields.structural_mediator: Formation of coherent Ti-rich nanoprecipitates within the L12 matrix.
fields.mechanism: Titanium has a strong tendency to form coherent precipitates in ordered matrices. In the L12 phase, its controlled precipitation can serve as effective obstacles to dislocation glide, thereby increasing the work-hardening rate and yield strength. Additionally, the dispersion of these nanoprecipitates can enhance the activation of multiple slip systems by locally modifying stress fields, which enhances ductility. This dual effect leverages a classical precipitation strengthening mechanism (as observed in maraging steels, TXT::wikipedia::Maraging_steel::008) while preserving a ductile matrix–reinforcement interaction.
fields.predicted_outcome: A simultaneous increase in yield strength and an improvement in ductility (via enhanced strain hardening) compared to the baseline alloy; the anticipated improvements are modest but significant when considering the delicate strength–ductility balance.
fields.baseline: The original AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy with no titanium addition and the reported two-phase eutectic microstructure.
fields.boundary: The beneficial effect should hold as long as titanium is added in a controlled manner to avoid excessive precipitation that can disrupt the lamellar arrangement or lead to embrittlement.
fields.uncertainty: The specific quantitative impact is uncertain and highly sensitive to the titanium content and aging parameters used for precipitate formation.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two sets of samples: one baseline and one with the specified titanium addition. After homogenization and any necessary aging, use TEM to verify the formation and coherence of Ti-rich nanoprecipitates in the L12 phase. Then, conduct tensile and compression tests at room temperature.
measurements: TEM for nanoprecipitate size and distribution in the L12 phase
Yield strength, tensile elongation, and work-hardening behavior from mechanical tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If titanium-added samples do not exhibit the formation of coherent precipitates in L12 or if there is no statistically significant improvement in both strength and ductility relative to the baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C5
pool.builds_on: The paper's findings on L12 precipitation strengthening combined with established improvements in Ni3Al ductility via boron doping.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes a minor alloying intervention (boron addition) in eutectic HEAs to enhance interfacial cohesion and ductility while preserving precipitate-based strengthening—a strategy not explored in the paper.

fields.hypothesis: Minor boron doping of the alloy enhances interfacial cohesion and refines precipitate nucleation, providing simultaneous improvement in strength and ductility.
fields.material_initial_state: An Al0.7CoCrFeNi eutectic high-entropy alloy with a lamellar fcc + B2 microstructure capable of precipitation hardening to form L12 precipitates.
fields.intervention: Introduce a small amount (around 0.3–0.5 at.%) of boron during melting to be uniformly distributed in the alloy.
fields.conditions: Applied along the standard processing route (homogenization, rolling, and low-temperature aging similar to the CR-H-580 condition), ensuring controlled boron segregation without forming brittle boride phases.
fields.structural_mediator: Boron segregation at grain boundaries and at the fcc/L12 precipitate interfaces, leading to enhanced bonding and refined precipitate distribution.
fields.mechanism: The addition of boron lowers the interfacial energy and suppresses crack initiation typical of highly ordered intermetallics. It can also alter nucleation kinetics, leading to finer, more coherent L12 precipitates that strengthen the matrix via an Orowan mechanism while improved interfacial cohesion mitigates premature fracture, increasing ductility.
fields.predicted_outcome: An improvement in yield strength on the order of the ~300 MPa increase observed with L12 precipitation and an additional 10–15% boost in ductility relative to undoped samples.
fields.baseline: The conventional CR-H or CR-H-580 processed Al0.7CoCrFeNi alloy without boron addition.
fields.boundary: Excess boron could result in deleterious boride formation; thus, optimal doping levels must be maintained to avoid embrittlement.
fields.uncertainty: While the strengthening effect is reasonably anticipated, the exact magnitude of ductility enhancement is moderately uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Al0.7CoCrFeNi alloys—one with ~0.3–0.5 at.% boron and one without. Process both identically through homogenization, rolling, and aging at 580°C for 24 hours. Conduct quasi-static tensile tests and analyze interfacial microstructures with TEM.
measurements: Yield strength
Ultimate tensile strength
Elongation to failure
TEM analysis of interface integrity and precipitate morphology
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-doped sample does not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in ductility (≥10% increase) while maintaining or exceeding the strength of the undoped sample, the hypothesis will be refuted.

pool.label: C6
pool.builds_on: The established understanding that lamellar spacing critically influences mechanical properties in eutectic systems, as discussed in the paper and supported by broader eutectic alloy literature.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes a completely different processing route—rapid solidification—to refine the microstructure of eutectic HEAs, a strategy not investigated in the paper, to achieve a dual improvement in mechanical behavior.

fields.hypothesis: Rapid solidification processing refines the lamellar spacing, thereby increasing interface density to simultaneously enhance strength and ductility.
fields.material_initial_state: A conventionally cast Al0.7CoCrFeNi eutectic high-entropy alloy exhibiting a relatively coarse lamellar microstructure with fcc and B2 phases.
fields.intervention: Employ rapid solidification methods (such as melt spinning) to achieve high cooling rates (on the order of 10^5 K/s), followed by a short, mild annealing below 600°C to relieve residual stresses without significant coarsening.
fields.conditions: The rapid solidification must achieve a refined lamellar spacing while preserving the intended phase compositions, and the annealing step must be carefully controlled to avoid loss of the refined microstructure.
fields.structural_mediator: A finer lamellar microstructure with a higher density of fcc/B2 interfaces and a more uniform distribution of phases, which can also foster the formation and uniform distribution of nano-twins during deformation.
fields.mechanism: Refined lamellar spacing increases the area of interfaces, which act as barriers to dislocation motion (enhancing strength via Orowan-like mechanisms) and distribute strain more homogeneously, reducing localized stress concentrations that lead to failure. The increased interface density also provides favorable sites for the nucleation of deformation-induced nano-twins, which further improves ductility by accommodating strain.
fields.predicted_outcome: An increase in yield strength by approximately 15–20% relative to conventionally cast samples, and an improvement in elongation (ductility) by at least 10% due to more homogeneous deformation.
fields.baseline: Eutectic HEAs produced through conventional casting and homogenization, as characterized in the paper.
fields.boundary: Extremely high cooling rates might induce non-equilibrium phases; the subsequent annealing must avoid excessive grain growth while retaining the refined structure.
fields.uncertainty: Exact quantification of ductility improvement is uncertain because rapid solidification may introduce residual stresses that also affect mechanical behavior.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one using conventional casting/homogenization and the other using rapid solidification (melt spinning) followed by a brief sub-600°C annealing. Use microscopy to measure lamellar spacing and perform tensile tests to determine strength and ductility.
measurements: Lamellar spacing distribution
Yield strength
Elongation to failure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the rapid solidification samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in lamellar spacing accompanied by at least a 10% improvement in both strength and ductility compared to conventional samples, the hypothesis is refuted.

pool.label: C7
pool.builds_on: The mechanism of strain-partitioning and hierarchical microstructure formation in cryo-deformation as reported in the paper.
pool.what_is_new: It proposes a completely different severe plastic deformation method (cryogenic HPT) rather than cryo-rolling, leveraging shear-dominated strain gradients to achieve simultaneous strength and ductility enhancement.

fields.hypothesis: Cryogenic high-pressure torsion (HPT) processing will generate a refined, heterogeneous shear microstructure in eutectic HEAs that simultaneously increases strength and ductility.
fields.material_initial_state: As-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy (e.g. AlCoCrFeNi2.1) with a dual-phase lamellar structure.
fields.intervention: Process the alloy using high-pressure torsion at cryogenic temperatures (in liquid nitrogen) to impart severe shear deformation.
fields.conditions: Perform HPT at liquid nitrogen temperature under high hydrostatic pressure with several rotation cycles to achieve an equivalent strain comparable to the cryo-rolling case.
fields.structural_mediator: Formation of ultra-fine shear bands, gradient sub-grain structures, and a heterogeneous distribution of deformation between the soft (L12/FCC) and hard (B2) phases, with abundant geometrically-necessary dislocations at phase boundaries.
fields.mechanism: The severe shear imposed by cryogenic HPT enhances strain partitioning between phases, leading to a hierarchical microstructure. The ultrafine sub-grains in the softer phase improve yield strength via the Hall–Petch effect while the maintained coarse, less-strained regions (especially in B2) provide nucleation sites for dislocation pile-ups that generate significant back stress, delaying necking and thus improving ductility.
fields.predicted_outcome: An increase in yield and ultimate tensile strength by approximately 20–30%, with either maintained or slightly enhanced elongation to failure compared to the as-cast baseline.
fields.baseline: As-cast eutectic HEA without severe deformation processing.
fields.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold for eutectic HEAs with inherent phase contrast; extreme torsional strains or overprocessing that could homogenize the microstructure might negate the beneficial gradient effects.
fields.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of improvement and optimal torsion parameters need refinement; effects may vary with alloy composition and processing details.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of eutectic HEA samples: one processed by cryogenic HPT and one kept as-cast. Perform tensile testing and microstructural characterization (TEM/EBSD) on both sets.
measurements: Yield strength
Ultimate tensile strength
Elongation to failure
Grain size distribution
Phase deformation states
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the cryogenic HPT-treated samples do not exhibit both a statistically significant increase in strength (∼20–30% improvement) and maintained or improved ductility relative to the as-cast samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C8
pool.builds_on: the finding in the paper that an alternating soft fcc/hard B2 lamellar structure leads to ultrahigh strain hardening and unique mechanical performance.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes a targeted interstitial modification (oxygen addition) to explicitly modify dislocation behavior within the eutectic structure, an intervention not explored in the paper.

fields.hypothesis: Minor oxygen complexing in the fcc phase of the eutectic high-entropy alloy will enhance work hardening by transitioning dislocation motion from planar to wavy slip, thereby simultaneously increasing strength and ductility.
fields.material_initial_state: The as-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, currently exhibiting high ductility from the soft fcc phase and high strength from the hard B2 phase.
fields.intervention: Introduce a controlled, trace addition of oxygen during melting to promote the formation of ordered oxygen complexes specifically within the fcc regions.
fields.conditions: Maintain conventional casting conditions but introduce oxygen (e.g., as a controlled O2 partial pressure or oxide flux adjustment) to achieve oxygen contents at trace levels (~0.05‐0.1 wt.%).
fields.structural_mediator: Formation of oxygen complexes at dislocations within the fcc phase and at the fcc/B2 interfaces.
fields.mechanism: The ordered oxygen complexes act as obstacles to dislocation glide, causing a transition from planar slip to wavy slip which facilitates multiple cross-slips. This mechanism enhances strain hardening without sacrificing ductility, as dislocation interactions are modified favorably. This approach builds on previous work showing similar effects in refractory high-entropy alloys where ordered oxygen complexes improved dislocation behavior (TXT::wikipedia::Strengthening_mechanisms_of_materials::035).
fields.predicted_outcome: An increase in both yield strength and tensile ductility relative to the baseline EHEA; the improvement magnitude is expected to be modest (potentially a 10–20% increase in work hardening rate), though precise quantitative gains have uncertainty.
fields.baseline: The original AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA with no intentional oxygen addition exhibiting ~944 MPa fracture stress and ~25.6% elongation at room temperature.
fields.boundary: The positive effects should persist as long as oxygen levels remain in the trace regime; excessive oxygen leading to oxide inclusions could be detrimental.
fields.uncertainty: The precise oxygen content threshold and spatial distribution are experimentally determined parameters that may vary; excessive oxygen may lead to embrittlement if not controlled.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of otherwise identical AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEAs: one with trace oxygen addition (~0.05–0.1 wt.%) and one control without added oxygen. Ensure identical casting and thermal processing conditions. Conduct standard tensile tests at room temperature and elevated temperatures, as well as microstructural analysis (TEM/APT to detect oxygen complex formation).
measurements: Tensile yield strength, fracture strength, and elongation
Strain hardening rate from engineering/true stress–strain curves
Microstructural evidence of oxygen complex formation via TEM or atom probe tomography
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the oxygen-added samples do not show a statistically significant improvement (e.g., >10% higher yield strength and/or elongation) along with evidence of modified dislocation slip compared to controls, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C9
pool.builds_on: the underlying principle from NiAl-based alloys where boron improves ductility by reinforcing grain boundaries, combined with the eutectic concept utilized in the paper.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis extends the compositional tuning strategy by introducing boron into a eutectic HEA to specifically target interfacial integrity—a parameter not explored in the reported paper.

fields.hypothesis: Adding a minor amount of boron to the composition of the eutectic high-entropy alloy will enhance interfacial cohesion and suppress inter-lamellar decohesion, leading to simultaneous improvements in strength and ductility.
fields.material_initial_state: The as-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with sharp fcc/B2 interphase boundaries that may be prone to decohesion under stress.
fields.intervention: Introduce a small boron addition (e.g., ~0.1–0.3 atomic %) into the alloy composition during melting.
fields.conditions: Maintain all other compositional and processing parameters constant; the only change is the addition of boron in controlled amounts during alloy preparation.
fields.structural_mediator: Boron segregation at fcc/B2 phase boundaries and grain boundaries.
fields.mechanism: Boron is known from studies in NiAl-based systems to segregate to grain boundaries and improve ductility by mitigating brittleness (TXT::wikipedia::Nickel_aluminide::001). In the eutectic HEA, boron is expected to segregate to the fcc/B2 interfaces, reducing interface energy and preventing premature decohesion. This enhanced bonding at the phase interfaces under tensile loading enables more effective load sharing, improving both strength (via reduced interfacial failure) and ductility (by delaying crack initiation and propagation).
fields.predicted_outcome: A simultaneous increase in tensile strength and ductility relative to the baseline alloy; predicted improvements might be on the order of 10–15% though precise bounds are uncertain without further data.
fields.baseline: The standard AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA without boron addition as reported in the paper.
fields.boundary: The benefits are expected as long as boron remains in a minor concentration; too high a concentration could lead to formation of brittle boride phases.
fields.uncertainty: Precise boron concentration windows and the extent of interfacial modification need careful experimental calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Melt and cast two batches of the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA: one with the target boron addition (0.1–0.3 at.%) and a control batch without boron. Conduct detailed microstructural analysis to confirm boron segregation at interfaces and perform tensile tests at room and elevated temperatures.
measurements: Tensile yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation
Interface characterization via high-resolution microscopy and chemical analysis (EDS, atom probe)
Phase analysis to ensure no undesirable boride phases have formed
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If boron-added samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in both strength and ductility compared to the control, or if brittle borides form and deteriorate properties, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C10
pool.builds_on: The paper demonstrated that tailoring microstructure (via phase-selective recrystallization) can enhance ductility; this hypothesis extends that principle by altering the chemistry of the critical boundaries.
pool.what_is_new: Instead of only using mechanical processing (PSR) to manipulate microstructural strain partitioning, this intervention employs minor alloying (boron doping) to modify the interphase and grain-boundary chemistry, targeting both strength and ductility improvement through suppressed cracking.

fields.hypothesis: Trace boron doping in eutectic HEAs will improve both strength and ductility by enhancing grain boundary cohesion and suppressing premature intergranular fracture.
fields.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with a dual-phase (FCC and skeletal B2) microstructure in the as-cast or lightly processed state.
fields.intervention: Introduce a small addition (typically 0.1–0.5 at%) of boron into the alloy during melting.
fields.conditions: Maintain the conventional melting and casting process, followed by standard thermomechanical treatment (e.g., a single cycle of moderate cold rolling and annealing) so that the only new variable is the boron addition. The processing temperature and cooling rates remain similar to those used in the referenced study.
fields.structural_mediator: Enhanced grain boundary chemistry with boron segregation that strengthens the boundaries and reduces the nucleation of cracks, while potentially refining the grain size slightly.
fields.mechanism: Boron is known to segregate to grain boundaries and reduce their energy, thereby enhancing intergranular cohesion. This minimizes early cracking and delay crack propagation during deformation. In addition, by inhibiting excessive grain growth during annealing, boron helps retain a finer microstructure that improves yield strength. Together, these effects boost both the strain hardening ability and ductility.
fields.predicted_outcome: Tensile tests should show a significant increase in both uniform elongation (potentially 20–30% relative increase over the untreated baseline) and ultimate tensile strength (a similar order of or modest improvement compared to conventional processing).
fields.baseline: EHEAs processed via conventional hot deformation or full recrystallization (AC/FR states) without boron addition as reported in PMC9365806.
fields.boundary: This effect is expected to hold for eutectic HEAs with a comparable dual-phase FCC/B2 structure; success may be limited if the alloy chemistry or phase distribution does not favor boron segregation.
fields.uncertainty: The exact effective concentration and distribution of boron and its potential for forming brittle boride phases must be carefully controlled; quantitative improvements are subject to optimization.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of the eutectic HEA: one with the trace boron addition and one without. Process both under identical conditions (moderate rolling and annealing). Conduct uniaxial tensile tests at room temperature and perform fractographic and atom probe analyses to check for boron segregation at grain boundaries.
measurements: Tensile true stress–strain curves (yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, uniform elongation)
Fracture surface characteristics by SEM
Chemical mapping of grain boundaries (e.g., atom probe tomography or EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-doped alloy does not show statistically significant improvements in both ductility and strength compared with the undoped alloy, or if brittle phases form that deteriorate the mechanical properties, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C11
pool.builds_on: The referenced paper shows that modifying the deformation and annealing pathway (through PSR) enhances ductility; here, the mechanism is extended to achieving a bimodal grain structure through flash annealing that targets both strength and ductility.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis deviates from phase-selective recrystallization by using a very rapid, high-temperature annealing cycle to tailor a bimodal microstructure, rather than relying solely on differential recovery/recrystallization of the two phases.

fields.hypothesis: Rapid, flash annealing after moderate deformation can create a bimodal grain structure—with an ultrafine grain (UFG) fraction embedded in a coarser, continuous B2 skeletal framework—that synergistically enhances both strength and ductility in eutectic HEAs.
fields.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with a cast duplex microstructure (FCC and skeletal B2 phases) as produced by conventional processing.
fields.intervention: Implement a rapid flash annealing treatment (very high heating rate, short dwell time, and immediate quench) following a moderate cold rolling reduction (approximately 30%) instead of the standard annealing cycle.
fields.conditions: After a moderate deformation step at room temperature, flash anneal the alloy at a high temperature (close to but below full recrystallization of the B2 phase) for a very short time (seconds to one minute), then quench rapidly in water. This process should preserve substructure in the B2 phase while allowing selective recrystallization in portions of the FCC phase.
fields.structural_mediator: A bimodal grain size distribution where ultrafine, recrystallized FCC grains provide high strength through grain boundary strengthening, while the retained coarse, continuous B2 phase maintains connectivity and ductility by reducing overall grain boundary density.
fields.mechanism: The flash annealing creates a non-equilibrium microstructure: rapid heating allows partial recrystallization in the softer phase, while the hard B2 phase only undergoes limited recovery without extensive recrystallization. The resulting microstructure combines the benefits of grain refinement (increased strength via Hall–Petch effect) and a continuous load-bearing phase that sustains ductility through enhanced strain partitioning.
fields.predicted_outcome: Tensile testing should show improvements in both strength (likely a 10–20% increase in yield/ultimate tensile strength) and uniform ductility (an increase in elongation similar to or exceeding that achieved by PSR), compared to samples subjected to standard annealing treatments.
fields.baseline: Conventional PSR-treated or fully recrystallized eutectic HEAs as reported in PMC9365806.
fields.boundary: The success of the flash annealing is contingent on precise control of the heating rate and time to selectively recrystallize only part of the microstructure; too long an annealing may lead to unwanted full recrystallization.
fields.uncertainty: Optimization of the flash annealing parameters is critical; there is some uncertainty regarding the reproducibility of the bimodal grain structure, and quantitative performance improvements need careful evaluation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sample groups: one subjected to the rapid flash annealing treatment after moderate deformation and one treated by the standard annealing schedule used in PSR. Characterize the grain structure via EBSD/TEM to verify a bimodal distribution and perform tensile tests to assess mechanical properties.
measurements: Grain size distribution analysis (EBSD/TEM)
Tensile stress–strain curves (yield strength, UTS, elongation)
Fracture surface morphology by SEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the flash annealed samples do not exhibit a clear bimodal grain structure and if there is no concurrent improvement in both strength and ductility relative to the control, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C12
pool.builds_on: the finding in PMC8368001 that atomic SRO yields a pseudo-composite microstructure (with hard and soft clusters) that can simultaneously enhance strength and ductility
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis extends the simulation insights to a eutectic HEA system by using a controlled, brief post-solidification anneal to induce SRO uniformly across both eutectic phases without altering the lamellar morphology.

fields.hypothesis: A brief, low‐temperature post‐solidification homogenization anneal applied to a eutectic HEA having nearly identical phase compositions can induce atomic-level short-range ordering (SRO) within each lamellar phase, yielding a pseudo-composite microstructure that improves both strength and ductility.
fields.material_initial_state: A eutectic HEA fabricated by conventional casting in which the two eutectic phases have similar elemental distributions and a largely random, un-ordered atomic arrangement.
fields.intervention: Apply a short-duration, low-temperature homogenization anneal (e.g., at ~0.3–0.4 Tm for a few minutes) immediately after solidification.
fields.conditions: Annealing must be performed in an inert atmosphere at a temperature low enough to prevent coarsening of the lamellar structure but high enough to enable limited atomic diffusion; the alloy must be designed so that both eutectic phases are compositionally similar to allow SRO to develop in each.
fields.structural_mediator: Development of atomic-scale SRO clusters (e.g., regions with FCC-preferred and BCC-preferred local ordering) within each lamellar domain, preserving a fine, interpenetrating pseudo-composite microstructure.
fields.mechanism: The post-solidification anneal permits limited atomic rearrangement while maintaining the eutectic morphology. This induces SRO similar to that observed in PMC8368001, where FCC-preferred clusters behave as hard, dislocation-resisting fillers and BCC-preferred clusters accommodate localized strain via reversible phase transformation. This combination raises the yield/ultimate strength while allowing for improved plasticity.
fields.predicted_outcome: Relative to the as-cast eutectic HEA baseline, the annealed specimens are expected to show simultaneous increases in ultimate tensile strength and tensile ductility (with improvements possibly on the order of 10–20%, though exact amounts will depend on the alloy system and annealing parameters).
fields.baseline: Eutectic HEA produced by conventional casting with a nearly random atomic arrangement and no significant SRO.
fields.boundary: The intervention is effective only if the annealing temperature and duration are carefully optimized; too high a temperature or overly long anneal may lead to lamellar coarsening or unwanted precipitation that could be detrimental.
fields.uncertainty: Exact improvement percentages are system-dependent and require experimental calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of eutectic HEA samples: one set as-cast (baseline) and one subjected to the designed low-temperature homogenization anneal. Characterize atomic-scale ordering using high-resolution TEM and atom probe tomography (APT) to detect SRO features, and perform tensile tests at room temperature to measure strength and ductility.
measurements: High-resolution TEM/APT for detecting SRO clusters within the lamellae.
Tensile stress–strain curves to extract ultimate tensile strength, yield strength, and elongation.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not exhibit measurable SRO (e.g., formation of distinct FCC-preferred and BCC-preferred clusters) or if both the strength and ductility do not statistically exceed those of the as-cast baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C13
pool.builds_on: the insights from TMP-induced microstructural tuning in Co-rich TRIP-HEAs (PMC9267696) combined with established solute drag mechanisms (as in maraging steels, TXT::wikipedia::Maraging_steel::005) to influence eutectic microstructure formation.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis integrates a precise, simulation-guided minor compositional modification (Mo addition) during solidification to achieve interface pinning and eutectic refinement in HEAs—a single intervention strategy different from the post-cast thermomechanical processing methods explored in the referenced paper.

fields.hypothesis: An optimized minor addition of molybdenum (Mo), guided by thermodynamic simulations to around 0.5–1.0 at%, will segregate to eutectic interfaces during solidification, pinning the interfaces to refine eutectic spacing and stabilize coherent boundaries, thereby simultaneously increasing strength and ductility.
fields.material_initial_state: A eutectic HEA fabricated by conventional casting, which typically develops relatively coarse and heterogeneous eutectic structures with some incoherent interfaces that limit the balance between strength and ductility.
fields.intervention: Incorporate a precise and small amount of Mo (approximately 0.5–1.0 at%) into the alloy composition during melting, as determined optimal by preliminary thermodynamic modeling and atomistic simulations.
fields.conditions: The alloy should be melted, homogenized, and cast under an inert atmosphere with standard cooling protocols. The Mo content must be strictly controlled to ensure it mainly segregates to the eutectic interfaces rather than forming separate Mo-rich phases.
fields.structural_mediator: A refined eutectic microstructure in which Mo segregates at the phase boundaries, generating a solute drag (or Smith–Zener pinning) effect that retards interface migration, leading to finer, more coherent eutectic lamellae.
fields.mechanism: The minor addition of Mo is expected to preferentially segregate to the eutectic phase boundaries during solidification, where it exerts a solute drag effect that pins these interfaces and prevents coarsening—a proven mechanism in high-performance alloys (TXT::wikipedia::Maraging_steel::005). This refined and stabilized interface network serves as an effective barrier to dislocation motion (akin to grain boundary strengthening) while maintaining or even enhancing ductility by minimizing stress concentrators from incoherent regions.
fields.predicted_outcome: A simultaneous improvement in yield strength (estimated in the range of 15–25% higher than the Mo-free alloy) and maintenance or slight enhancement in tensile ductility, compared to the baseline eutectic HEA.
fields.baseline: Conventional eutectic HEA samples without Mo addition, which form coarser eutectic structures with partial incoherency at phase boundaries, leading to a compromised trade-off between strength and ductility.
fields.boundary: The intervention’s success hinges critically on the precise Mo content; if the Mo level is too high, deleterious Mo-rich phases may form and embrittle the alloy, while too little Mo may fail to produce the desired pinning effect.
fields.uncertainty: Although solute drag and interface pinning by minor Mo additions are well-established, the exact quantitative improvements in this specific eutectic HEA system are uncertain and require experimental confirmation guided by thermodynamic prediction.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of eutectic HEA samples using identical casting procedures: one set with the standard composition and the other incorporating 0.5–1.0 at% Mo. Utilize TEM/SEM and compositional analysis (e.g., EDS or atom probe tomography) to examine eutectic spacing and verify Mo segregation at interfaces. Perform tensile testing to compare yield strength and ductility.
measurements: TEM/SEM imaging of eutectic lamellae and phase boundary structure
EDS/atom probe analysis to detect Mo segregation and confirm absence of Mo-rich precipitates
Mechanical testing (tensile stress–strain curves) to evaluate yield strength and elongation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Mo-doped samples do not exhibit a statistically significant refinement of the eutectic spacing with predominantly coherent interfaces and fail to show simultaneous improvements in yield strength (≥15% gain) and ductility relative to the baseline, or if deleterious Mo-rich phases are detected, the hypothesis is falsified.

fields.hypothesis: Introduce a minor alloying modification by adding a small fraction (e.g., ∼0.5 wt.%) of titanium (Ti) to the standard CoCrFeNiMn HEA composition to reduce stacking fault energy, thereby promoting beneficial nano twin formation during rapid solidification and achieving simultaneous improvements in both strength and ductility.

fields.intervention: Adjust the alloy composition by adding approximately 0.5 wt.% Ti into the feedstock through careful blending and pre-alloy processing such as high-energy ball milling, ensuring a homogeneous distribution of Ti before SLM processing.
fields.conditions: The alloy with the Ti addition should be processed under the same SLM conditions (laser power, scanning speed, protective atmosphere) as the baseline alloy. fields.uncertainty: Although the mechanism of stacking fault energy reduction and twin promotion via minor alloying is well established in other systems, the specific quantitative effect in eutectic HEAs processed by SLM remains to be fully determined.

top3.builds_on: the insights from TMP-induced microstructural tuning in Co-rich TRIP-HEAs (PMC9267696) combined with established solute drag mechanisms (as in maraging steels, TXT::wikipedia::Maraging_steel::005) to influence eutectic microstructure formation.
top3.what_is_new: This hypothesis integrates a precise, simulation-guided minor compositional modification (Mo addition) during solidification to achieve interface pinning and eutectic refinement in HEAs—a single intervention strategy different from the post-cast thermomechanical processing methods explored in the referenced paper.

fields.hypothesis: An optimized minor addition of molybdenum (Mo), guided by thermodynamic simulations to around 0.5–1.0 at%, will segregate to eutectic interfaces during solidification, pinning the interfaces to refine eutectic spacing and stabilize coherent boundaries, thereby simultaneously increasing strength and ductility.
fields.material_initial_state: A eutectic HEA fabricated by conventional casting, which typically develops relatively coarse and heterogeneous eutectic structures with some incoherent interfaces that limit the balance between strength and ductility.
fields.intervention: Incorporate a precise and small amount of Mo (approximately 0.5–1.0 at%) into the alloy composition during melting, as determined optimal by preliminary thermodynamic modeling and atomistic simulations.
fields.conditions: The alloy should be melted, homogenized, and cast under an inert atmosphere with standard cooling protocols. The Mo content must be strictly controlled to ensure it mainly segregates to the eutectic interfaces rather than forming separate Mo-rich phases.
fields.structural_mediator: A refined eutectic microstructure in which Mo segregates at the phase boundaries, generating a solute drag (or Smith–Zener pinning) effect that retards interface migration, leading to finer, more coherent eutectic lamellae.
fields.mechanism: The minor addition of Mo is expected to preferentially segregate to the eutectic phase boundaries during solidification, where it exerts a solute drag effect that pins these interfaces and prevents coarsening—a proven mechanism in high-performance alloys (TXT::wikipedia::Maraging_steel::005). This refined and stabilized interface network serves as an effective barrier to dislocation motion (akin to grain boundary strengthening) while maintaining or even enhancing ductility by minimizing stress concentrators from incoherent regions.
fields.predicted_outcome: A simultaneous improvement in yield strength (estimated in the range of 15–25% higher than the Mo-free alloy) and maintenance or slight enhancement in tensile ductility, compared to the baseline eutectic HEA.
fields.baseline: Conventional eutectic HEA samples without Mo addition, which form coarser eutectic structures with partial incoherency at phase boundaries, leading to a compromised trade-off between strength and ductility.
fields.boundary: The intervention’s success hinges critically on the precise Mo content; if the Mo level is too high, deleterious Mo-rich phases may form and embrittle the alloy, while too little Mo may fail to produce the desired pinning effect.
fields.uncertainty: Although solute drag and interface pinning by minor Mo additions are well-established, the exact quantitative improvements in this specific eutectic HEA system are uncertain and require experimental confirmation guided by thermodynamic prediction.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of eutectic HEA samples using identical casting procedures: one set with the standard composition and the other incorporating 0.5–1.0 at% Mo. Utilize TEM/SEM and compositional analysis (e.g., EDS or atom probe tomography) to examine eutectic spacing and verify Mo segregation at interfaces. Perform tensile testing to compare yield strength and ductility.
measurements: TEM/SEM imaging of eutectic lamellae and phase boundary structure
EDS/atom probe analysis to detect Mo segregation and confirm absence of Mo-rich precipitates
Mechanical testing (tensile stress–strain curves) to evaluate yield strength and elongation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Mo-doped samples do not exhibit a statistically significant refinement of the eutectic spacing with predominantly coherent interfaces and fail to show simultaneous improvements in yield strength (≥15% gain) and ductility relative to the baseline, or if deleterious Mo-rich phases are detected, the hypothesis is falsified.

top3.label: C11
top3.builds_on: The referenced paper shows that modifying the deformation and annealing pathway (through PSR) enhances ductility; here, the mechanism is extended to achieving a bimodal grain structure through flash annealing that targets both strength and ductility.
top3.what_is_new: This hypothesis deviates from phase-selective recrystallization by using a very rapid, high-temperature annealing cycle to tailor a bimodal microstructure, rather than relying solely on differential recovery/recrystallization of the two phases.

fields.hypothesis: Rapid, flash annealing after moderate deformation can create a bimodal grain structure—with an ultrafine grain (UFG) fraction embedded in a coarser, continuous B2 skeletal framework—that synergistically enhances both strength and ductility in eutectic HEAs.
fields.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with a cast duplex microstructure (FCC and skeletal B2 phases) as produced by conventional processing.
fields.intervention: Implement a rapid flash annealing treatment (very high heating rate, short dwell time, and immediate quench) following a moderate cold rolling reduction (approximately 30%) instead of the standard annealing cycle.
fields.conditions: After a moderate deformation step at room temperature, flash anneal the alloy at a high temperature (close to but below full recrystallization of the B2 phase) for a very short time (seconds to one minute), then quench rapidly in water. This process should preserve substructure in the B2 phase while allowing selective recrystallization in portions of the FCC phase.
fields.structural_mediator: A bimodal grain size distribution where ultrafine, recrystallized FCC grains provide high strength through grain boundary strengthening, while the retained coarse, continuous B2 phase maintains connectivity and ductility by reducing overall grain boundary density.
fields.mechanism: The flash annealing creates a non-equilibrium microstructure: rapid heating allows partial recrystallization in the softer phase, while the hard B2 phase only undergoes limited recovery without extensive recrystallization. The resulting microstructure combines the benefits of grain refinement (increased strength via Hall–Petch effect) and a continuous load-bearing phase that sustains ductility through enhanced strain partitioning.
fields.predicted_outcome: Tensile testing should show improvements in both strength (likely a 10–20% increase in yield/ultimate tensile strength) and uniform ductility (an increase in elongation similar to or exceeding that achieved by PSR), compared to samples subjected to standard annealing treatments.
fields.baseline: Conventional PSR-treated or fully recrystallized eutectic HEAs as reported in PMC9365806.
fields.boundary: The success of the flash annealing is contingent on precise control of the heating rate and time to selectively recrystallize only part of the microstructure; too long an annealing may lead to unwanted full recrystallization.
fields.uncertainty: Optimization of the flash annealing parameters is critical; there is some uncertainty regarding the reproducibility of the bimodal grain structure, and quantitative performance improvements need careful evaluation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sample groups: one subjected to the rapid flash annealing treatment after moderate deformation and one treated by the standard annealing schedule used in PSR. Characterize the grain structure via EBSD/TEM to verify a bimodal distribution and perform tensile tests to assess mechanical properties.
measurements: Grain size distribution analysis (EBSD/TEM)
Tensile stress–strain curves (yield strength, UTS, elongation)
Fracture surface morphology by SEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the flash annealed samples do not exhibit a clear bimodal grain structure and if there is no concurrent improvement in both strength and ductility relative to the control, the hypothesis is falsified.

top3.label: C10
top3.builds_on: The paper demonstrated that tailoring microstructure (via phase-selective recrystallization) can enhance ductility; this hypothesis extends that principle by altering the chemistry of the critical boundaries.
top3.what_is_new: Instead of only using mechanical processing (PSR) to manipulate microstructural strain partitioning, this intervention employs minor alloying (boron doping) to modify the interphase and grain-boundary chemistry, targeting both strength and ductility improvement through suppressed cracking.

fields.hypothesis: Trace boron doping in eutectic HEAs will improve both strength and ductility by enhancing grain boundary cohesion and suppressing premature intergranular fracture.
fields.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with a dual-phase (FCC and skeletal B2) microstructure in the as-cast or lightly processed state.
fields.intervention: Introduce a small addition (typically 0.1–0.5 at%) of boron into the alloy during melting.
fields.conditions: Maintain the conventional melting and casting process, followed by standard thermomechanical treatment (e.g., a single cycle of moderate cold rolling and annealing) so that the only new variable is the boron addition. The processing temperature and cooling rates remain similar to those used in the referenced study.
fields.structural_mediator: Enhanced grain boundary chemistry with boron segregation that strengthens the boundaries and reduces the nucleation of cracks, while potentially refining the grain size slightly.
fields.mechanism: Boron is known to segregate to grain boundaries and reduce their energy, thereby enhancing intergranular cohesion. This minimizes early cracking and delay crack propagation during deformation. In addition, by inhibiting excessive grain growth during annealing, boron helps retain a finer microstructure that improves yield strength. Together, these effects boost both the strain hardening ability and ductility.
fields.predicted_outcome: Tensile tests should show a significant increase in both uniform elongation (potentially 20–30% relative increase over the untreated baseline) and ultimate tensile strength (a similar order of or modest improvement compared to conventional processing).
fields.baseline: EHEAs processed via conventional hot deformation or full recrystallization (AC/FR states) without boron addition as reported in PMC9365806.
fields.boundary: This effect is expected to hold for eutectic HEAs with a comparable dual-phase FCC/B2 structure; success may be limited if the alloy chemistry or phase distribution does not favor boron segregation.
fields.uncertainty: The exact effective concentration and distribution of boron and its potential for forming brittle boride phases must be carefully controlled; quantitative improvements are subject to optimization.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of the eutectic HEA: one with the trace boron addition and one without. Process both under identical conditions (moderate rolling and annealing). Conduct uniaxial tensile tests at room temperature and perform fractographic and atom probe analyses to check for boron segregation at grain boundaries.
measurements: Tensile true stress–strain curves (yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, uniform elongation)
Fracture surface characteristics by SEM
Chemical mapping of grain boundaries (e.g., atom probe tomography or EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-doped alloy does not show statistically significant improvements in both ductility and strength compared with the undoped alloy, or if brittle phases form that deteriorate the mechanical properties, the hypothesis is falsified.
